Water is running down the car-park ramp. Your laptop is in a basement locker. What now?
Go down quickly while the water still looks shallow.
Ask a neighbour to bring it up for me.
Stay out of the basement, warn the manager, and follow emergency advice.
That’s the safer choice. Never enter a flooding basement or garage to retrieve belongings. Move valuables in advance, only while conditions are safe.
Less guessing. One clear next step.
Read the whole warning, including its location and action statement. Flooding can develop before a warning reaches you.
The warning says “Prepare to evacuate”. Your usual riverside shortcut is under water.
Follow official instructions, organise an early safe departure and use a dry, open route.
Walk through if other people are doing it.
Wait for a neighbour to post a video before deciding.
Yes. Act on the warning, check that your route is dry and open, and leave early when advised and safe. Never walk, ride or drive through floodwater. If trapped or in immediate danger, call 000.

This path is for people with disability and their carers. You can do it together or independently, pause whenever you like, and choose what applies to you.
What makes an apartment flood plan useful?
It assumes everyone can use the stairs without help.
It covers my access, communication, equipment and chosen support people.
It relies on my usual carer always being available.
Yes. Your preferences lead the plan. Include backup people and options if your usual support or transport is unavailable.
You know what works for you.
Select any topics you want to think through. There is no need to share a diagnosis. Carers: ask the person how they want to be supported.
Your usual support person cannot reach the building. What helps most?
A backup contact, accessible transport plan, and agreed check-in method.
Assuming someone will notice and come to help.
Leaving the plan until the power has already failed.
Exactly. Agree who will check in, how they will contact you, and who takes over if they cannot help. Get their agreement in advance.
Plan for the things a power cut changes.
Lifts are only one part of the picture. Find out what depends on electricity in your building and in your day.
Does being registered for life support guarantee uninterrupted power?
Yes, it guarantees power and an immediate rescue.
No. I still need a backup plan with my clinician, equipment provider, and support people.
Yes, as long as my building has a generator.
Correct. Registration does not guarantee continuous supply. Confirm a safe backup duration and relocation plan with your providers. If a power failure puts your life at risk, call 000.
Pack for your everyday needs, too.
Start with the shared essentials. Then add the items that support your mobility, communication, health, comfort, or assistance animal.
Know the way. Know who can help.
A building walk is a good time to check real features together. The presence of a lift, refuge or backup generator must be confirmed for your building.
You cannot use stairs and the lift is out. What should your plan cover?
Neighbours carrying me downstairs without a planned method.
Waiting in any stairwell and assuming someone will find me.
An agreed assistance procedure, a designated safe waiting location if the building has one, and a way to communicate my exact location.

Yes. Agree a personal evacuation plan with the building team and your support people in advance. Do not improvise carrying or use an evacuation chair without trained help. If there is immediate danger, call 000 and explain your location and assistance needs.
You decide what to record and who to share it with. Use this as a conversation starter for a person-centred emergency plan.
Include your regular medicines, a medicine list and prescriptions. Ask your pharmacist about safe storage and your personal supply needs.
Plan for at least three days of food and drinking water at home. Choose ready-to-eat food and a can opener; pack a manageable amount to carry.
Keep a working torch handy. Avoid candles because of fire risk.
Mobile networks can fail. A radio and spare batteries give you another way to hear updates. ABC Melbourne: 774 AM.
Keep copies of your ID, rental details, contacts and insurance information in a waterproof pouch, with keys and some cash if possible.
Charge devices before bad weather and keep the right cables together. Write key contacts on paper too.
Add a first-aid kit, hygiene items, warm clothes, glasses and what you need each day. Plan for children, pets or an assistance animal.
Leave these out. Choose a torch or battery light to reduce fire risk.
A grab bag needs to be manageable. Plan bulky valuables ahead of time; do not delay leaving to move furniture.
Never use a camping stove, barbecue or generator indoors, in a garage, or another enclosed space. They can cause carbon monoxide poisoning.
Check step-free entrances and an alternative if the lift fails. Agree accessible transport, who can help, and how far ahead you need to leave.
Choose text, speech, Easy Read, Auslan or another format that works for you. Keep a paper communication card and a way to get warnings if internet or power fails.
List powered equipment, charging needs and supplier contacts. Ask your clinician and supplier about compatible backups, battery duration and medicine refrigeration.
Plan eating, drinking, personal care and rest. Pack sensory or comfort items and agree how your usual support can continue somewhere else.
Include food, water, medication, identification and a lead or harness. Check how your animal will travel and stay with you at your chosen destination.
Keep your grab bag close to the exit without blocking it. Learn your stair and exit locations. Save building contacts and agree a check-in with someone you trust.
Move important papers and electronics off low shelves where practical.
Check your contents cover and record photos of belongings. Ask your insurer about flood cover.
Ask the building manager where warnings are shared, who is the emergency contact after hours, and where the building plan is displayed.
Confirm exits and the outdoor assembly point in the building plan.
A fire assembly point may be unsuitable in a flood. Follow the current flood advice.
Ask what stops working in a power cut: lifts, doors, intercoms and water pumps.
Before flooding, while it is safe, move valuables out of basement storage. A waterproof tub is useful for splashes but is not a guarantee against a flooded basement.
Do not store essential medicines, passports or your only emergency kit downstairs.
Move a car or bike early only if safe and consistent with building advice.
Once water is entering, stay out. Report it to the manager; do not go back for belongings.
Floodwater may contain sewage, chemicals and debris. Wait for authorities and the building team to confirm safe access before returning to affected spaces.
Keep food sealed and rubbish bins closed to discourage rats and mice.
Report rodents, droppings, damaged wiring or mould to building management. Arrange safe cleanup and pest control.
Do not use flood-damaged electrical equipment until it has been professionally checked.

Lifts can stop. Powered doors, intercoms and garage access may also fail. Ask management about safe manual access and the procedure when lifts are unavailable. Do not use a lift during flooding unless emergency personnel specifically direct you.

Backup power must suit your equipment. Ask your clinician and equipment provider what to do, how long the backup lasts, and when to relocate. Do not assume a building generator powers your apartment or device.

Wi-Fi, mobile networks and powered alert systems may fail. Keep paper contacts, a charged power bank and an agreed offline check-in plan. Ask your personal alarm provider how their system behaves without power.

Pumps, hot water, refrigeration, heating and cooling may stop. Plan drinking water, ready-to-eat food and temperature needs. Ask a pharmacist about refrigerated medicines; follow official food-safety advice.
